source.title: Accurate Neural Network Pruning Requires Rethinking Sparse Optimization
source.authors: Denis Kuznedelev; Eldar Kurtic; Eugenia Iofinova; Elias Frantar; Alexandra Peste; Martin Jaggi

record.tranche_reason: The study reports its own sparse-training results. These qualify the broad claim: sparse vision models can keep improving with extended training, while sparse transfer models can move from undertraining to overfitting. It does not test dense networks from random initialization as described in the versions.
record.gate_note: The paper tests sparse optimization and training duration, not whether sufficiently large dense networks from random initialization reach near-zero classification error. Sparse training results are relevant qualifications to the broad claim. Cited results from prior work are not extracted as rows.
record.test_reason: The study tests sparse optimization and transfer recipes, but none of V1–V6. It reports validation accuracy, training cross-entropy, prediction uncertainty and loss-landscape properties without the comparisons or outcomes required by these versions. Its discussion of progressive sharpening does not measure a stability threshold or demonstrate V5's dynamics.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that standard dense recipes generally undertrain sparse models; extended and adapted recipes improve sparse vision training, while sparse BERT transfer also requires controlling overfitting. They motivate more efficient sparsity-aware optimization.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies high-sparsity training with AC/DC, RigL, GMP, and sparse BERT transfer recipes. It varies sparse-training duration and pruning schedules; it does not reproduce the dense random-initialization experiments in the listed versions.
record.method_sensitivity: Sparse-training outcome varies with sparsity and training duration; vision models benefit from extended training, while sparse language transfer can move from undertraining to overfitting. AC/DC, RigL, and GMP have different accuracy and loss trajectories. Weight decay changes sparsity and accuracy.

fits_no_version.finding: Sparse ImageNet models require longer schedules to reach their best validation accuracy; 95% and 98% models remain unsaturated at 500 epochs in Figure 1.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Higher sparsity can increase the training duration needed for good validation performance under the tested sparse-training recipes.

fits_no_version.finding: On Celeb-A, optimal duration increases with sparsity, while training loss and prediction uncertainty decrease with longer training.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sparse vision models can require longer training before reaching their best validation performance.

fits_no_version.finding: Extended sparse-training schedules improve ImageNet results, with outcomes depending on method, sparsity and which layers remain dense.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sparse optimization recipes and training budgets affect the achievable sparsity–validation-accuracy tradeoff.

fits_no_version.finding: Sparse BERT transfer can move from undertraining to overfitting; the text states that training loss reaches zero while validation accuracy falls.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Extending dense transfer recipes for sparse pretrained BERT requires task-dependent control of undertraining and overfitting.

fits_no_version.finding: Section 3.8 reports increasing endpoint sharpness with training duration, lower sharpness at higher sparsity, and loss barriers between sparse checkpoints. It does not compare sharpness with a learning-rate stability threshold.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sparse-training duration and sparsity affect endpoint sharpness and checkpoint interpolation barriers.

record.problems: The principal sparse-vision duration curves are figure-only, with exact values unavailable in text. Many comparison-table numbers are reported from cited prior papers rather than runs conducted in this study. The experiments do not measure the claim versions' core training classification-error outcome on CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100.
record.rows_left_out: Cited results from prior methods were omitted from rows because the paper identifies them as previously reported literature. Further per-task GLUE metrics and per-method figure-only curves are not exhaustively itemized; they do not measure any listed version.

untested.parts: Near-zero CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100 training classification error, including random or corrupted labels, and its dependence on model size, stopping and regularization.
Two-layer ReLU teacher-student local minima and the effect of one or two extra student neurons.
Training-error degradation with depth, identity-shortcut comparisons, and the stated initialization and normalization exceptions.
Activation-matched initialization, signal and gradient propagation, orthogonal versus Gaussian weights, and trainable depth.
Recovery above the initial stability limit, catapult dynamics, full-batch sharpness relative to the stability threshold, and divergence.
Batch-normalization comparisons for training speed and learning-rate tolerance, and Fixup comparisons.

record.verdict_notes: Replace the reader's T5 classification: these results do not qualify a listed version merely because they concern optimization. CIFAR datasets in Appendix F are downstream transfer evaluations, not V1 training-error experiments. Section 3.8's reference to progressive sharpening is insufficient to test V5. E3's displayed paraphrase concerns performance deterioration below a loss/entropy level, rather than the unsaturated high-sparsity result attributed to R3–R4.

versions.untested_parts: Dense networks from random initialization; CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100 training error; random or corrupted labels; model size and early stopping.
Teacher-student two-layer ReLU problems, spurious minima, and student width relative to teacher width.
Plain versus residual depth comparisons and the effects of shortcuts, special initialization, or normalization on training error.
Initialization comparisons for signal or gradient propagation, learning speed, and trainable depth.
Learning rates above stability limits, catapult dynamics, sharpness thresholds, and divergence.
Batch normalization comparisons for training speed or learning-rate tolerance, including Fixup residual networks.
